title: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of different regions can be explained by their climate and other physical conditions; regions with closely parallel conditions (e.g. Australia, South Africa and western South America at 25°–35° S) have utterly different faunas and floras.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the first great fact which strikes us is, that neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of various regions can be accounted for by their climatal and other physical conditions.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XI, “Geographical Distribution”; section “Present distribution cannot be accounted for by differences in physical conditions”. Scope: terrestrial and marine faunas and floras of the world's major regions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch11-01: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.83

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Global occurrence and environmental datasets directly enable the stated comparison at large scale. Causal partitioning of history and environment is imperfect, but the strong claim is readily testable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Model global assemblage taxonomic and phylogenetic similarity from climate and physical environment, then compare environmentally matched regions on different continents. The absolute wording is refuted if conditions explain most biotic similarity and supported if strong regional residuals remain.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:

Occurrence sampling is geographically biased.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Community dissimilarity, climate distance, and region identity are standard variables in two open global sources. Variation partitioning can be run for plants and vertebrates at the regional scale the claim uses. Sampling bias is real and is handled by restricting the test to well-sampled cells and higher taxa.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Partition compositional dissimilarity among the world's regions into a climate component and a regional component, including matched southern temperate belts. If climate distance accounts for which regions share their biotas, the claim fails.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Occurrence data are denser in some countries, which can exaggerate regional differences.

Present climate omits the conditions lineages experienced in the past.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.75
data existence: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.8

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Across regions of the world, the taxonomic similarity of their biotas is explained by which land mass they belong to (shared history and barriers) rather than by the similarity of their climates; in particular, climatically matched regions on different continents (e.g. the Mediterranean-climate belts of Australia, South Africa and Chile) share fewer taxa than climatically different regions on the same continent.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Genus lists for Mammalia, Aves and Tracheophyta were obtained for the 23 pre-registered 5x5 degree regions from GBIF genus facets (genera with >= 3 georeferenced, non-flagged, present records); climate was summarised from NASA POWER climatology at five points per box (annual mean T2M, annual precipitation, seasonal temperature range), standardised (log precipitation) and converted to Euclidean climate distance. Pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity (253 pairs) was regressed on climate distance and a same-continent indicator with a Mantel-type permutation test (2000 permutations of region labels), and partial R-squared values compared; separately, the mean similarity of climate-matched cross-continental pairs was compared with climate-mismatched same-continent pairs. Central Arabia was dropped for mammals (17 genera < 20).

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. For the 23 regions in derived/regions.csv (5x5 degree boxes, pre-assigned to a continent and to one of six climate classes), genus lists of mammals, birds and vascular plants are taken from GBIF occurrences (genera with >= 3 georeferenced records in the box), and climate from the NASA POWER climatology (annual mean 2 m temperature, annual precipitation, seasonal temperature range at five points per box). For each taxon group, pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity between regions is regressed on standardised climate distance and a same-continent indicator (permutation test over region labels, 2000 permutations). The claim is SUPPORTED if, in at least 2 of the 3 taxon groups, (a) the same-continent effect is significant (p < 0.05) and its partial R-squared exceeds that of climate distance, and (b) the mean Jaccard similarity of climate-matched pairs on different continents is lower than the mean similarity of climate-mismatched pairs on the same continent.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if, in at least 2 of the 3 taxon groups, climate distance has the larger partial R-squared and the same-continent effect is not significant, or climate-matched cross-continental pairs are more similar than climate-mismatched same-continent pairs. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. If GBIF returns fewer than 20 genera for a region/group, that region is dropped for that group; if fewer than 15 regions remain for a group, the group is not evaluated.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: taxon groups (of 3) in which same-continent membership outweighs climate distance and climate-matched cross-continental pairs are less similar than climate-mismatched same-continent pairs

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: permutation p-values per group in extra

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'inhabitants of various regions' are read as the genus-level composition of three well-recorded groups (Mammalia, Aves, Tracheophyta); 'climatal and other physical conditions' as the NASA POWER temperature and precipitation climatology; 'similarity' as Jaccard similarity of genus lists. His 'accounted for' is read comparatively: climate distance should explain less of the variation in biotic similarity than does being on the same land mass, and his own example (Australia, South Africa, western South America at 25-35 degrees S) is tested directly as the climate-matched cross-continental pairs. The absolute wording ('neither ... nor ... can be accounted for') is not testable as stated because climate obviously limits distributions within a continent; the comparative reading is the one tested. Regions and climate classes were fixed before any data were retrieved. GBIF records include introduced species, which inflate cross-continental similarity and therefore work against the claim.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
GBIF occurrence search API (genus facets within bounding boxes)

NASA POWER climatology API (temporal/climatology/point)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
For vascular plants the result is reversed: climate distance explains more of the genus-level dissimilarity (partial R2 0.36) than continent (0.08), although the same-continent effect is still significant and climate-matched cross-continental pairs are still (non-significantly) less similar than mismatched same-continent pairs. Genus-level plant composition is strongly shared across continents (cosmopolitan and Holarctic genera, plus introduced species in GBIF), so the claim holds for mammals and birds but not, at genus rank, for plants.

GBIF occurrences include introduced and vagrant taxa and uneven sampling; the >= 3 record filter removes only the rarest. Introduced species inflate cross-continental similarity and bias the test against the claim.

Climate is summarised by three variables from a 0.5 degree reanalysis-based climatology at five points per box; finer climatic structure (soils, topography) is not represented. The 'same continent' indicator also absorbs geographic distance, which Darwin treated as part of the same explanation (barriers and history).

Darwin's own triad (SW Australia, Western Cape, central Chile) shares a mean of 16% of mammal genera and 24% of bird genera, versus 30% and 57% for climatically different regions on the same continent.

The absolute wording of the claim is not tested; the comparative reading (continent outweighs climate) is.
